title: Why do I feel overwhelmed by everything? What helps when it all feels like too much
description: Why many small demands feel larger together than apart — demands judged against resources, unfinished goals that stay switched on, attention residue and switching costs — and what helps in order: one complete list, a next step and a time for every item, one thing at a time with a ready-to-resume note, shrinking the list on purpose, and ten minutes of writing the worry itself.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

Nothing on the list is huge. An email. A form. A message you owe someone. A bill, a deadline, a small decision you keep postponing. And yet the whole pile feels impossible, your chest tightens, and you cannot start any of it — so you scroll, or freeze, and then you blame yourself for freezing. If you have searched "why do I feel overwhelmed by everything" or "I can't cope, it's all too much", this guide is for that moment. It sets out what the research actually shows about why many small demands feel larger together than they are apart, what helps in the order most people can use it, and where an app fits — including ours, with our measured numbers printed as they are.

We are Anicca. We make a small affirmation app, and stress and overthinking are among the struggles people can choose inside it. This guide is not an ad and it is not treatment. Feeling overwhelmed is not, by itself, a diagnosis.

## Why does everything feel like too much at once?

Three things make a pile of small demands feel like one large threat.

**First, overwhelm is a judgement about demands and resources, not a count of tasks.** In their foundational account, Lazarus and Folkman (1984) defined psychological stress as a relationship between a person and their environment that the person appraises as taxing or exceeding their resources and endangering their well-being. The same list can feel manageable on a rested morning and impossible after a bad night, not because the list changed, but because the resources you can bring to it — sleep, time, help, certainty — did change. That is why "just organise it better" misses the point. The useful question is not only "how much is there?" It is also "what resource is missing right now: time, information, help, or rest?"

**Second, unfinished goals stay switched on, and they compete with whatever you are trying to do now.** Masicampo and Baumeister (2011a) showed across several studies that unfulfilled goals produced intrusive thoughts during an unrelated reading task, kept goal-related words highly accessible, and lowered performance on an unrelated anagram task. In companion work, Masicampo and Baumeister (2011b) reported five studies in which an unfulfilled goal impaired later tasks that required executive function — solving anagrams and logic problems — while sparing a test of general knowledge that did not require that function. In plain terms: each open item is not resting quietly in the background. Part of your attention is still holding it, and that part is not available for the task in front of you. Ten open items do not feel like ten small things. They feel like one mind divided ten ways.

**Third, switching itself costs, and the cost grows with complexity.** In four experiments, Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans (2001) found that people lost time on every switch between tasks, that the loss grew when the tasks were more complex or less familiar, and that the switch has two stages: shifting the goal, and activating the rules for the new task. The individual costs were small — fractions of a second in the laboratory — and they added up across repeated switching. You may have seen a claim that switching can cost up to 40% of productive time. That figure is an estimate attributed to Meyer in a summary by the American Psychological Association; it is not a measurement reported in the 2001 paper itself, and this guide does not present it as one. The honest finding is narrower and still useful: switching is never free, and a day built out of switches will feel harder than the same work done in sequence.

There is a fourth piece, and it explains why an unfinished task follows you into the next one. Leroy (2009), in two experiments, named it attention residue: when people moved from an unfinished task to a new one, part of their attention stayed with the first task, and their performance on the new task suffered. Finishing the first task helped, but finishing it without really disengaging was not, on its own, enough. Step 3 below is built on this work and on its follow-up.

## What helps, in the order most people can use it

These steps do not remove the demands. Nothing honest can promise that. They change the two things the research says you can change in the moment: how many goals are switched on at once, and whether each open goal has a plan that lets your mind set it down.

### 1. Get it all out of your head and onto one list — do not sort it yet

Write every demand down in one place, exactly as it arrives in your mind: the email, the fear about the email, the form, the thing you are avoiding, the decision. Do not organise, prioritise or solve anything in this step. The point is externalisation — moving the holding work out of working memory and onto paper or a screen, where it can be seen all at once.

The writing evidence is about worries specifically, and it is measured. Klein and Boals (2001) ran two semester-long experiments with college students. In the first, 35 freshmen who wrote about their thoughts and feelings about coming to college showed larger working-memory gains seven weeks later than 36 students who wrote about a trivial topic. In the second, students who wrote about a negative personal experience (n = 34) showed greater working-memory improvements and declines in intrusive thinking than students who wrote about a positive experience (n = 33) or a trivial topic (n = 34). The authors' account is that writing about a stressful experience reduces intrusive and avoidant thinking about it, which frees working-memory resources. A list is not expressive writing, and this guide does not claim the same effect for a list. What the two share is the direction: what is written down no longer has to be held in the same way. Sort the list only after it is complete — sorting while you are still remembering is one more switch.

### 2. Give every unfinished thing a next step and a time — a plan, not a finish

Go through the list and, for each item, write two things only: the next physical step ("open the form and fill in the first page", not "sort the form"), and when you will do it. Leave the rest of each task undesigned. This step feels too small to matter. In the research, it is the step that mattered most.

Masicampo and Baumeister (2011a) found that allowing participants to formulate specific plans for their unfulfilled goals eliminated the activation and interference effects described above — the intrusive thoughts stopped and performance recovered — even though the goals themselves were still unfulfilled. The reduction depended on how earnestly participants committed to their plans: the people who later carried their plans out were the people who showed no more intrusions. A plan is therefore not a wish and not a longer list. It has to name a step you actually intend to take, at a time that actually exists. Once that is written, the research suggests, the drive that keeps the goal switched on can be suspended until the time arrives, and resumed then. You have not finished ten things. You have given ten things a place to wait that is not your attention.

### 3. Do one thing at a time — and leave a ready-to-resume note when you switch

Choose the one item whose deadline or consequence is nearest, and work only on it until you reach the step you planned, or until a set, short period ends. Silence the inputs that would switch you: close the other tabs, put the phone in another room if you can, and let messages wait. This is not a moral rule about focus. It follows directly from the switching costs above (Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans, 2001) and from attention residue (Leroy, 2009): every switch charges you twice, once to leave and once to reload.

Life will interrupt anyway. When it does, use the repair that Leroy and Glomb (2018) tested across four studies in *Organization Science*. People who expected to resume an interrupted task under time pressure showed high attention residue and performed worse on the interrupting task — and a brief "ready-to-resume" plan mitigated the effect. Before you switch, write one line: where you stopped, and what the first action will be when you return. ("Stopped after paragraph two. Next: add the dates from the letter.") It takes less than a minute, and it gives the unfinished task the same thing Step 2 gave the whole list: a specific place to wait.

### 4. Shrink the list on purpose — say what will not happen today

A list with a plan for every item can still be longer than a day. Overwhelm returns if the plan quietly assumes you will do all of it today. So make the subtraction explicit. Mark each item as today, this week, or not mine / not now — and for anything you move, tell the person who is waiting, in one short message, when they will hear from you. Moving an item with a message sent is a completed step. Moving it silently is a new open goal, and it will behave like one.

This step is also where the first section's question returns: which resource is missing? If the honest answer is help, the next step for that item is asking for it, by name, with a specific request. If the answer is information, the next step is the one message or search that gets it. If the answer is rest, no ordering of the list will substitute for sleep, and the kindest accurate plan for tonight may be the smallest one: eat, prepare one thing for the morning, and stop. Lazarus and Folkman's (1984) account cuts both ways — demands can be reduced, and resources can be restored, and a plan that only ever works on the demand side will keep failing on the days when you are depleted.

### 5. Write the worry itself down for ten minutes — then close the page

Sometimes the list is done, the plans are written, and the feeling is still there, circling one feared outcome: the reply will be angry, the result will be bad, you have already failed. That circling is a worry, not a task, and it does not respond to another look at the list. Give it its own ten minutes, on paper, in sentences: what you fear, what it would mean, what you would do next if it happened. Then close the page and return to the one task from Step 3.

The closest measured version of this is Ramirez and Beilock (2011), in *Science*: two laboratory studies and two randomised field experiments in which students wrote about their worries about an upcoming exam immediately before taking it. The brief writing — ten minutes in the classroom work — significantly improved exam scores, especially for students who were habitually anxious about tests. In the laboratory work, students who sat quietly dropped in accuracy under pressure, while students who wrote did not show the same drop; in the field work, the most anxious students improved by nearly a grade point. The setting was examinations, not a whole life arriving at once, and this guide does not claim the same size of effect for a hard day. The mechanism the authors propose is the one this step borrows: worries occupy working memory, and writing them down gives them somewhere else to be while you work.

If you repeat one small version of these steps daily — one list, one plan, one thing at a time — expect it to become easier slowly, not this week. In the habit research this guide cites throughout, Lally and colleagues (2010) found that a new daily behaviour took a median of 66 days to become automatic, with a wide range of 18 to 254 days, and that missing a single day did not materially affect the process. An overwhelmed day is not a failed system. It is one day.

## Where do apps fit in this?

An affirmation app cannot shorten your list, answer the email, or restore a night of sleep. What it can do, at most, is supply the words that are hardest to produce yourself in the moment your resources are lowest — a short, believable sentence that names the one next step instead of the whole pile. Used that way, it belongs inside Step 3: read one card, then do the one thing. Used as a way to scroll instead of starting, it becomes one more switch, and the research above predicts exactly what that will cost.

What to check before you rely on any app for this: whether you can choose the struggle you are in (stress, overthinking, a hard day) rather than receiving the same generic lines as everyone else; whether the words are sized to be believed on a bad day — "I can do the next step" rather than "I can do anything"; whether it reaches you during the day, when the demands arrive, instead of only when you remember to open it; and what it costs, in full, after any trial. Anicca is built around those choices: you pick the struggles, and short cards on those topics arrive through the day. That is a design claim, not a result. The measured part is the next section.

## Our own numbers, printed as they are

Anicca is small, and we publish the smallness. When we checked in November 2026, its US App Store listing showed 5.0 stars from 1 rating, and its Japanese listing 4.5 stars from 48 ratings. App Store Connect recorded 1 first download for Anicca in the 7 days to 12 November 2026. Premium is $59.99 a year on the US listing. If social proof is what you need — and for something you open on your most overwhelmed days it is a reasonable thing to need — larger apps have it and we do not, yet. What we can claim is only the design: a short card, on the topic you chose, arriving while the day is happening — not a shorter list arriving with it.

## When is feeling overwhelmed a sign to get human help?

If feeling overwhelmed is there most days for weeks, if you are falling behind on work, safety, money or relationships despite trying, if your sleep is broken and your mood stays low, treat that as a reason to talk to a clinician or a counsellor, not to download more software. Persistent overwhelm can be part of depression, an anxiety disorder, ADHD, burnout, a thyroid or other physical condition, or a load in your life — caring, debt, an unsafe situation — that deserves its own support and cannot be planned away by one person alone. If the load itself is the problem, help with the load is the treatment-shaped answer: a manager, a doctor, a debt adviser, a person you trust. If you ever feel that you might act on thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line in your country now — in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency; in the US, call or text 988. An article — including this one — is information, not assessment, and it is not a plan for your whole life.

## Common questions

### Why do I feel overwhelmed even when each task is small?

Because the cost is not only in the tasks. Each unfinished goal stays cognitively active and competes for the executive function you need for the task in front of you (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011b), and every switch between them charges a further cost that grows with complexity (Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans, 2001). Ten small open items can therefore consume more attention than one large closed one. The repair matches the mechanism: give each item a plan (Step 2) and work on one at a time (Step 3).

### Why can't I just push through and finish everything?

Sometimes you can, for a day. The research problem is what pushing through usually looks like: rapid switching, no plans, and unfinished items accumulating residue into each next task (Leroy, 2009). Effort spent that way buys less finished work per hour, which lengthens the list, which raises the feeling. Lazarus and Folkman's (1984) account adds the other half: if the missing resource is sleep or help, effort alone does not restore it. Finishing the nearest item completely, then the next, is slower to start and faster to finish.

### Should I make a longer to-do list to feel in control?

Make a complete list once — Step 1 — because unlisted items still occupy attention. But a longer list only helps if each item then gets a next step and a time (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011a). A detailed list of everything, with no plan attached, is a catalogue of unfulfilled goals, and the studies above predict it will keep intruding. Completeness first, planning second, length never for its own sake.

### Why do I keep thinking about unfinished tasks at night?

Because the goals are still switched on. Unfulfilled goals produced intrusive thoughts even during an unrelated task in the laboratory (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011a), and at night there is no next task to compete with them. The practical version of the finding is Steps 2 and 3 done before bed: write each open item's next step and time, and leave a ready-to-resume line for the task you stopped mid-way (Leroy & Glomb, 2018). You are not solving the items at night. You are giving them a place to wait until morning.

### How long should I try these steps before judging whether they help?

Judge the steps on whether the list gets shorter and the circling gets quieter over two to three weeks of most days — not on one bad afternoon. For the habit underneath them, Lally and colleagues (2010) measured a median of 66 days for a new daily behaviour to become automatic, ranging from 18 to 254 days, with a single missed day making no material difference. If weeks of trying leave you further behind, or the feeling is constant, that is information for the "get human help" section above, not a verdict on your effort.

### Can an affirmation app fix feeling overwhelmed?

No. An app cannot reduce your demands, restore your resources, or treat depression, anxiety, ADHD or burnout, and any app that promises to fix overwhelm is claiming more than the evidence in this guide supports. What an app can do is small and specific: put one believable sentence in front of you at the moment starting feels impossible, so that Step 3 — one thing, now — is easier to begin. If it does that, it has done its whole job.
